clue.text: "O snail, I beseech, speed or spurt! Oh calamity!" Why? Do I hear 3 23?

annotation.answer: THERE'S A PORPOISE CLOSE BEHIND US

definitions.note: a cryptic pointer to a line of Lewis Carroll, not a synonym

indicators.note: a calamity is a disaster, so the preceding words are wrecked and rebuilt in a new order

blocks.clueFragment: O snail, I beseech, speed or spurt!
blocks.note: all twenty-six letters of the plea are used
the exclamation's two letters join the fodder

explanation.surface: Someone frantically begs a snail to hurry, and wonders whose voice this is.
explanation.walkthrough: 3 23 is LOUIS CAROL, which sounds like Lewis Carroll. In his Lobster Quadrille a whiting urges a snail to walk faster because THERE'S A PORPOISE CLOSE BEHIND US: that answers 'Why?'.
explanation.definitionFit: The line is the whiting's reason for hurrying the snail in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, written by Lewis Carroll.

clue.text: Desertion from a job, say? Possibly

indicators.note: possibly suggests one of several arrangements, so the word before it is reordered

blocks.note: a job is a post
the three letters of say rearranged

explanation.surface: Walking out on one's employment might, perhaps, be called this.
explanation.definitionFit: Apostasy is the abandonment of a religious or political faith, a desertion of one's principles.

clue.text: He commissioned Corelli in "Les Bourrées", I gathered

indicators.note: fabric that is gathered is bunched and pleated, so these letters are bunched into a new order

blocks.note: fourteen letters taken together, accent ignored

explanation.surface: A patron seems to have hired the baroque composer Corelli to write some French dances.
explanation.walkthrough: Louis de Bernières wrote Captain Corelli's Mandolin; the grid omits 'de'. Corelli looks like the Italian composer, and bourrées are dances, but the commission is a military rank.
explanation.definitionFit: The novelist created Captain Corelli, so in a punning sense he gave the officer his army commission.

clue.text: See 1
Clash with St Paul's uncharitable tinkler

blocks.note: first meaning: a percussion disc that is crashed against its partner
second meaning: in 1 Corinthians 13, a man without charity is as a tinkling instrument

explanation.surface: A quarrel breaks out with a stingy bell-ringer at St Paul's Cathedral.
explanation.walkthrough: St Paul looks like the London cathedral, but it is the apostle: 'though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal'.
explanation.definitionFit: Cymbals are struck together in a crash, and Paul's letter compares a loveless speaker to a tinkling one.

clue.text: Stockholders raising a bargain, not a fracas

indicators.note: in a down entry, raising lifts the letters so they read from bottom to top
not a tells the solver to leave out one letter A from the word that follows

blocks.note: a snip is a bargain
fracas loses one of its two As

explanation.surface: Shareholders push up the price of a cheap deal while avoiding any row.
explanation.walkthrough: Stockholders suggests investors; a stock is also a stiff wide cravat, held in place by a pin.
explanation.definitionFit: A stock is a formal neckcloth, and the ornamental pins that fasten such neckwear hold the stock in place.

clue.text: Legionaries blowing hot or cold

definitions.note: plural noun for the collective noun

indicators.note: things blowing about are tossed in the wind, so the letters are scattered and resettled

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
C is the abbreviation for cold, as on a tap

explanation.surface: Roman soldiers who can never make up their minds, now warm, now chilly.
explanation.definitionFit: A cohort was a tenth of a Roman legion, a body of several hundred soldiers.

clue.text: Seventh Age to support the minority

blocks.note: to second a motion is to support it
minority is the state of being a minor, under age

explanation.surface: A seventh age has arrived in which the political minority is backed.
explanation.walkthrough: In As You Like It, Jaques's seven ages of man end in 'second childishness and mere oblivion'.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's final stage of life is senile dotage, when the old become as helpless as infants again.

clue.text: No force in spin doctor's art: New York finds it mesmerising

definitions.note: a noun use: the act of mesmerising

indicators.note: in places the opening words inside the word for the spin doctor's craft

blocks.note: spin doctors deal in exaggerated publicity
taken as written
g is the symbol for gravitational force
standard abbreviation for the city or state

explanation.surface: Political spin carries no weight, yet Manhattan is captivated by it.
explanation.walkthrough: Force is G, the symbol for acceleration due to gravity, as in g-force. 'Mesmerising' is read as a noun: the act itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Hypnogeny is the inducing of a hypnotic trance, which is what mesmerising a subject does.

clue.text: See 1
His barber was 25, he noted  ...

blocks.note: surface: someone remarks that the man who cuts his hair comes from Spain
setter's reading: he set to notes, i.e. composed, an opera whose barber was from Seville

explanation.surface: A man mentions in passing that his hairdresser is Spanish.
explanation.walkthrough: 25 is SPANISH. 'Noted' looks like remarked, but here it means put into musical notes.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian composer wrote The Barber of Seville, whose title character Figaro works in Spain.

clue.text: ...  and his doctor had lawyers to see!

blocks.note: barristers collectively are the Bar
taken as written
lo is an old exclamation meaning look

explanation.surface: The same man's physician needed legal advice.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis carries 'his' over from the previous clue: Dr Bartolo is Rosina's guardian in The Barber of Seville.
explanation.definitionFit: In that opera the scheming physician Bartolo is the guardian who hopes to marry his ward Rosina.

clue.text: Fly-killer was making time

indicators.note: making means fashioning, so the letters are fashioned into a fresh order

blocks.note: taken as written
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Someone who kills flies was taking a while about it.
explanation.definitionFit: A swat is a flat implement for hitting insects, also called a flyswatter.

clue.text: Thick German plate smash-ed into dead pieces

indicators.note: something smashed is broken apart, so the letters of the plate are jumbled
broken into pieces, the letters before it fall into a new order
into puts the broken plate inside the other jumbled letters

blocks.note: D is the international car code for Germany
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A stupid German breaks a plate, smashing it to bits.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen in smash-ed is a nod to the hyphenated answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Addle-pated means muddle-headed or stupid, as is someone called thick in British slang.

clue.text: See 3
Unwaged? Don't spend so much!

blocks.note: first meaning: receiving no salary
second meaning: an instruction to hand over a smaller sum

explanation.walkthrough: Read as one word it is an adjective for unpaid; split as two it is advice to economise.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective it describes someone earning no salary; as a phrase it urges lower outlay.

clue.text: Sibelius was without a local angle

indicators.note: without here means outside, so one word wraps around the other

blocks.note: to angle is to fish
a local is a neighbourhood pub

explanation.surface: The composer Sibelius went without a hometown viewpoint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' reads as lacking but means outside. A local is British slang for one's regular pub.
explanation.definitionFit: Jean Sibelius was a native of Finland, the country's most celebrated composer.

clue.text: Feste's international dimension?

blocks.note: setter's reading: a cap marks an international appearance, so Feste's would be a jester's cap
the other reading: a traditional size of writing paper

explanation.surface: Wondering how Shakespeare's jester Feste measures up on the world stage.
explanation.walkthrough: Feste is the clown in Twelfth Night. A player chosen for their country wins a cap, and the old paper size is named after a jester's headgear watermark.
explanation.definitionFit: Foolscap is an old size of writing paper, and a jester's headgear is literally a fool's cap.

clue.text: Show one the ropes in it and knot a tie

indicators.note: to knot is to twist and tangle, so the letters following are twisted into another order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
the four letters rearranged

explanation.surface: Teaching a newcomer the knots: put it in and tie a tie.
explanation.definitionFit: To initiate someone is to introduce them to the basics of an activity, teaching them how things work.

clue.text: Hood and train for success donned here!

definitions.note: a phrase describing the place, standing for a noun

blocks.note: Robin Hood, the outlaw of Sherwood
to groom someone is to prepare them to succeed

explanation.surface: Hoods and trains, the trappings of a graduation or office, are put on in this room.
explanation.walkthrough: Hood and train double as garments: an academic hood and a robe's train are just what gets put on in such a room.
explanation.definitionFit: A robing room is the chamber where judges, clergy or graduates put on their ceremonial gowns.

clue.text: Rural guardian, unable to raise charges, is out of work: page her!

definitions.text: Rural guardian, unable to raise charges, is out of work: page her!

blocks.clueFragment: Rural guardian, unable to raise charges, is out of work
blocks.note: surface: a country official who cannot levy fees finds herself unemployed
setter's reading: a shepherdess who has lost her flock has nothing to tend, and a pager would bleep her

explanation.surface: A country warden who cannot collect her fees is laid off and must be summoned.
explanation.walkthrough: The charges are sheep, not fees: the nursery-rhyme shepherdess lost hers and doesn't know where to find them. 'Page her' hints at the peep or bleep of a pager.
explanation.definitionFit: Little Bo-Peep is the nursery-rhyme shepherdess who mislaid her sheep, leaving her with no flock to mind.

clue.text: Fraulein's in the arena! Terrific!

definitions.note: a German woman for her first name

indicators.note: in says the name sits inside the run of words that follows

blocks.note: found spanning the end of arena and the start of terrific

explanation.surface: A German girl is in the stadium and having a wonderful time.
explanation.definitionFit: Renate is a common German female first name, so it suits an unmarried German woman.

clue.text: An eminent figure in the history of the postal service

definitions.text: An eminent figure in the history of the postal service

blocks.note: surface: a distinguished person; setter's reading: a raised landform, an eminence

blocks.clueFragment: in the history of the postal service
blocks.note: the reformer who introduced the penny post and the adhesive stamp

explanation.surface: A distinguished person who shaped the history of the Post Office.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Rowland Hill introduced the Penny Black stamp in 1840; an eminence is also a piece of rising ground.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both Rowland, the British postal reformer, and a rise in the land, literally an eminence.

clue.text: Waits to sing this

blocks.note: surface: someone holds back before singing; setter's reading: waits are street singers at Christmas
what such seasonal singers perform door to door

explanation.surface: Someone pauses before launching into a song.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Waits' reads as a verb but is a noun: in Britain the waits were bands of Christmas street musicians.
explanation.definitionFit: A carol is a festive Christmas song, the traditional repertoire of the singers who went house to house.

clue.text: Gold prospector's instrument absorbing a man of music

indicators.note: absorbing means taking in, so the instrument holds the next piece inside it

blocks.note: or is the heraldic word for gold
prospectors swirl river gravel in a pan
a man is referred to as he

explanation.surface: A gold prospector's tool takes in a musician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A man of music' looks like one unit, but the definition is just 'of music'.
explanation.definitionFit: Orphean means relating to Orpheus, the legendary Greek singer, and hence melodious or musical.

clue.text: For such an omelette, pan is hot and square initially

definitions.note: a phrase pointing to the adjective

indicators.note: initially asks for the opening letter of each of the two words before it

blocks.note: first letter of square, which also goes at the front
taken as written
taken as written
first letter of hot

explanation.surface: A cook's tip: for this omelette the pan must be hot and square.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Initially' does double duty: it takes first letters of hot and square, and puts the square's S at the start.
explanation.definitionFit: A Spanish omelette is a thick potato tortilla, the classic egg dish named after Spain.

clue.text: Foreign masher married in Kent

indicators.note: in puts the word for married inside the abbreviation for the county's region

blocks.note: Kent is in south-east England
to wed is to marry

explanation.surface: A flirtatious foreigner gets married in the county of Kent.
explanation.walkthrough: A masher is an old word for a ladies' man, so a foreign one could be a Swede; the surface also teases the mashed root vegetable.
explanation.definitionFit: A Swede is a man from Sweden, and masher is dated slang for a dandy who chases women.

clue.text: Popular song in Waterfoot refreshed

indicators.note: refreshed means made over anew, so the place name is remade in another order

blocks.note: a village in Lancashire, taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A favourite tune gets a new lease of life in a Lancashire village.
explanation.walkthrough: Refreshed hints at a cuppa, apt for the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Tea for Two is a 1925 standard by Vincent Youmans, a much-recorded popular number.
